paras: The Nashville streetcar riot took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a Black crowd at a Republican rally on Cherry street in Nashville, Tennessee, seized the driver of a streetcar that had run over and killed an elderly Black man, Alfred King, and tried to lynch him. Police and a constable got the wounded driver, Benjamin Woodward, to jail, which citizens and soldiers then guarded against the crowd.

Republican legislative nominees were speaking to a large crowd on Cherry street when a streetcar passed through it at about 8:30 in the evening. The car knocked down Alfred King, described by the Milan Exchange as "an old and respected negro" and by the Morristown Gazette as "a prominent negro politician"; the wheels passed over his abdomen and he died about an hour later. The Milan Exchange attributed the accident to the car's mules running away in the crowded street.

According to the Nashville dispatch, nearly 1,000 Black people seized the driver, and "hundreds of knives and pistols were out." The Morristown Gazette said the crowd meant to lynch him, believing the running over of King had not been an accident. Constable Dowdey, himself described as colored, held the crowd back until police arrived, though he was cut and knocked down several times.

After the riot signal was rung, a large body of citizens covered the police as they took the driver away amid shouts of "hang him," "shoot him" and "throw him off the bridge." Woodward reached the jail with a broken finger and several knife wounds, and police officers were also knocked down. Hundreds remained near the scene threatening to break into the jail and hang him, and one short report said the crowd spent the night at the jail making occasional rushes to get in.

Citizens and soldiers guarded the jail, and the Milan Exchange reported only that the lynching was "prevented." No report of an inquest into King's death or of any charge against the driver or members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

The story reached northern papers by wire the next day, headed "Riot in Nashville" in the Daily Republican and "How a Riot Was Caused by a Horse Car Accident" with the subhead "The Driver's Narrow Escape" in the Portland Daily Press. A shorter version, run as "A Mob of Negroes," said only that the man was injured. Tennessee weeklies treated King more personally, the Milan Exchange in a column of state news a week later and the Morristown Gazette on November 15. The Morristown account credited "white citizens armed with pistols" along with the police for keeping the crowd at bay.

The early short wire said King was injured, while the fuller dispatch and the Milan Exchange said he died. The Portland printing named the driver Benjamin Woodward and later "Westwood" in the same story.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A Black crowd seized and wounded a streetcar driver, whose race no report states, after his car fatally ran over a Black man, and threatened to hang him; the driver was the target, so this was not anti-Black violence (A2, A7).
A crowd of nearly 1,000 seized the driver, cut him and shouted 'hang him', but police took him to jail alive (A2, A4); it was an attempted lynching, and no one was killed by the crowd (A6).
The Associated wire (A2, A4), the Milan Exchange (A6) and the Morristown Gazette (A7) agree that King was run over and that a crowd tried to lynch the driver, though A1 says the man was only injured.

accounts.label: Nashville wire
accounts.gist: A street car ran through the rally crowd, killing King; nearly 1,000 Black men seized the driver, who was rescued by a constable and police and jailed under guard while crowds threatened the jail.

accounts.label: Short wire
accounts.gist: A colored man was injured; a mob threatened to lynch the driver, who was jailed for protection, and spent the night making rushes on the jail.

accounts.label: Tennessee papers
accounts.gist: The Milan Exchange blamed runaway mules; the Morristown Gazette said the crowd believed the act deliberate and that police and armed white citizens kept the mob back.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the wire as 'Riot in Nashville' and 'How a Riot Was Caused by a Horse Car Accident', stressing knives, pistols and the driver's 'narrow escape'.
Tennessee weeklies described King respectfully and called the death an accident.
